issues.legal_issue: An arbitral tribunal must remain within its reference, and a court reviewing an award cannot set it aside on an objection that was not raised before the tribunal.
material_facts: The arbitration concerned the delay in issuing a traffic-restriction notification and the resulting effect on toll collection.
The State did not argue before the tribunal that it had no contractual obligation to issue the notification.
The courts below relied on the absence of such an obligation when setting aside part of the award.
issues.conclusion: The courts below erred in deciding an objection that the State had not raised before the tribunal. An arbitrator cannot decide matters beyond the reference, though a court may intervene where an award exceeds the reference or contains a jurisdictional error.
issues.legal_principle: An arbitral tribunal derives its authority from the reference and cannot materially enlarge its scope. A court may intervene under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 for an award that exceeds the reference or is patently illegal, including for jurisdictional error. In exceptional circumstances, a tribunal may examine the contract and statutory provisions where a party properly pleads that a demand exceeds them. The Court relied on Grid Corporation of Orissa Ltd. v. Balasore Technical School; Delhi Development Authority v. R.S. Sharma and Company; Associated Engineering Co. v. Government of Andhra Pradesh; and Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. SAW Pipes Ltd.

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: The proceeding challenges an arbitral award before a court.
predicates.objection_not_raised_before_tribunal: A party relies on an objection in court that it did not raise before the arbitral tribunal.

issues.definition: When an award is challenged and the objection relied on in court was not raised before the tribunal, the court cannot set aside the award on that objection.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for toll losses caused by delay in issuing a traffic-restriction notification does not extend to losses attributed to failure to enforce the notification after it has been issued.
material_facts: The tribunal found that the notification restricting traffic through the town had been delayed and awarded compensation for toll losses.

The tribunal also awarded losses attributed to the period after issuance, although the State had no responsibility to establish a police post or otherwise implement the notification in the manner claimed.
issues.conclusion: The contractor was entitled to the tribunal’s award of Rs. 26.34 lacs for the delay in issuing the notification, with 10% interest, if unpaid or unadjusted. An award for losses attributed to non-enforcement after issuance was not justified.
issues.legal_principle: The compensable delay concerned issuance of the notification; once it was issued, the State had no responsibility to establish a police post to implement it. The award for losses therefore could not extend to post-issuance non-enforcement.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and notification_was_delayed and notification_was_issued and state_had_no_enforcement_duty

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: The proceeding challenges an arbitral award arising from a contractual dispute.
predicates.notification_was_delayed: The public authority issued a required traffic-restriction notification later than the contractor claimed it should have.
predicates.notification_was_issued: The public authority eventually issued the traffic-restriction notification.
predicates.state_had_no_enforcement_duty: The public authority was not contractually responsible for the particular steps said to be necessary to enforce the notification.

issues.definition: When an award challenge concerns delayed issuance of a notification that was eventually issued, and the authority had no duty to take the asserted enforcement steps, compensation excludes losses attributed to the period after issuance.

issues.legal_issue: A concessionaire may collect toll from users of a road section that forms an integrated part of the project and is covered by the concession arrangements.
material_facts: The project was a single composite road project that included the section at issue, which had been widened and strengthened by the contractor.
The traffic data in the bid documents included traffic on that section.
At the pre-bid conference, the State clarified that users of the section would have to pay toll.
The concession agreement permitted fees to be charged from all persons using the project facilities.
issues.conclusion: The section was part of the integrated project, and the contractor was entitled to collect toll from its users. The tribunal was directed to determine the amount that could have been recovered from those users.
issues.legal_principle: The terms of the concession agreement, the bid documents and the pre-bid clarification showed that the section was included in the project and toll applied to its users. Clauses 5 and 7 of the concession agreement distinguished project facilities from a temporary service road used during construction.

predicates.toll_concession_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a concessionaire may collect toll from users of a road section.
predicates.road_section_is_part_of_integrated_proje: The road section was included in the project as a whole rather than being an unrelated or temporary service road.
predicates.concession_covers_all_project_users: The concession arrangements provide for toll collection from users of the project facilities.

issues.definition: In a toll-concession dispute, when a road section is part of the integrated project and the concession covers project users, the concessionaire may collect toll from users of that section.

issues.legal_issue: Toll collection is compensatory and does not entitle a contractor to recover amounts for construction or maintenance work that it did not perform or fund.
material_facts: The toll arrangement was intended to allow recovery of project costs, maintenance costs, interest and toll-collection expenses, not to augment public revenue.
The contractor had completed the first phase but had not undertaken the second phase, which included further repairs and maintenance.
The contractor sought compensation calculated by reference to the larger project amount, although it had not made the investment required for the second phase.
The parties had agreed that compensation would be worked out on the basis of investment made.
issues.conclusion: The contractor could not claim compensation for amounts it had not spent. The tribunal was directed to reconsider what could have been recovered from users of the included road section and the effect of the unperformed second phase on the contract as a whole.
issues.legal_principle: A toll is compensatory and must bear a reasonable relationship to the benefit and the costs incurred; it cannot be used as a source of revenue or collected to recover costs never spent. The governing notification limited toll collection to recovery of construction and maintenance costs, interest and collection expenses. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Devi Dayal Singh; State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas; Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India; and, on contractor damages and expected profits, Dwaraka Das v. State of Madhya Pradesh, A.T. Brij Paul Singh v. State of Gujarat, and ONGC v. SAW Pipes Ltd. The general availability of damages for breach did not permit recovery of unincurred project costs in this toll arrangement.

predicates.toll_recovery_dispute: The proceeding concerns recovery through toll collection under a project concession.
predicates.toll_is_cost_reimbursement: The toll arrangement permits recovery of project-related costs rather than serving as a revenue source.
predicates.contractor_did_not_perform_or_fund_work: The contractor failed to perform or fund work for which it seeks recovery.

issues.definition: When toll collection is intended to reimburse project costs and the contractor did not perform or fund the work claimed, the contractor cannot recover those unincurred costs.

issues.legal_issue: A court may vary an agreed interest rate in deciding the interest payable on an arbitral award, and the appropriate rate depends on the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The arbitral award fixed interest at 18%.
The courts below reduced the rate to 10%, relying on prevailing economic and banking conditions and a prior decision of the Supreme Court.
The contractor argued that the contract required a higher rate.
issues.conclusion: The reduction of the interest rate to 10% was upheld, and the Supreme Court declined to interfere.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Interest Act, 1978 empowers a court to award interest at a rate not exceeding the current rate and implies power to vary a contractually agreed rate. Post-award interest is procedural. The Court relied on Krishna Bhagya Jala Nigam Ltd. v. G. Harischandra Reddy and H.U.D.A. v. Raj Singh Rana, which explain that the rate should be fixed in light of the circumstances of each case rather than imposed uniformly.

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: The proceeding challenges a court's treatment of interest on an arbitral award.
predicates.court_is_reviewing_award_interest: The court is deciding what interest rate should apply to the award.
predicates.circumstances_support_lower_rate: The circumstances of the case, including prevailing economic and banking conditions, support a lower rate.

issues.definition: When a court reviewing interest on an arbitral award finds that the circumstances support a lower rate, it may reduce the agreed rate.
